summary: Describes version 1.1 of Ipsilon's General Switch Management Protocol, a general-purpose protocol that lets a controller set up and release connections on an ATM switch and read its status. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A remote control for a network switch: you can tell it to connect or disconnect lines, and ask how it is doing.

questions: how to control an atm switch with a protocol
how does gsmp control an atm switch
what is the gsmp adjacency protocol
what is a gsmp port session number
subtitle: Ipsilon's master-slave protocol for letting a controller set up connections on an ATM switch and watch its ports.

tldr.problem: A separate controller needs a standard way to manage an ATM switch: make and remove connections, manage ports, and read configuration and statistics.
tldr.mechanism: GSMP runs over a control virtual channel on an ATM link. The controller sends request messages, the switch answers with success or failure, and an adjacency protocol keeps both ends in sync.
tldr.outcome: The memo describes version 1.1 of the protocol and is informational only. It was updated by RFC 2297.

today: RFC 1987 is an Informational RFC and is not an Internet standard. It has been updated by RFC 2297.

sections.title: What GSMP Does
sections.content:
The General Switch Management Protocol (GSMP) is a general purpose protocol to control an ATM switch. A controller can establish and release connections, add and delete leaves on a point-to-multipoint connection, manage ports, and request configuration and statistics. The switch can also report asynchronous events, such as a link going down.

GSMP is asymmetric: the controller is the master and the switch is the slave. One controller can manage several switches by running separate instances over separate control connections.

A switch has ports, each one input port plus one output port. Virtual channels are identified by VPI/VCI. A connection is named by its input port and incoming VPI/VCI. Ports are named by a 32-bit number assigned by the switch, and each port also has a port session number, ideally random, that changes whenever the port comes back up. Requests with a wrong session number are rejected, which lets the controller notice link failures.
sections.eli5: One boss computer tells a switch what to do. The switch only answers and never gives orders, except to say when something broke.

sections.title: Packet and Message Format
sections.content:
GSMP messages are carried directly in AAL-5 CPCS-PDUs with an LLC/SNAP header (octets AA AA 03 00 00 00 88 0C). The MTU of a GSMP message is 1500 octets. The default virtual channel is VPI 0, VCI 15.

Every message except the adjacency protocol has a common header: Version (currently 1), Message Type, Result, Code and a Transaction Identifier that ties a response to its request. The Result field is NoSuccessAck (1) or AckAll (2) in requests, and Success (3) or Failure (4) in responses. NoSuccessAck means the switch replies only on failure, which reduces traffic when the controller is just re-checking state.

Four request-response classes exist: connection management, port management, statistics and configuration. Event messages are sent by the switch and are not acknowledged. No GSMP message other than adjacency messages may be sent until the adjacency protocol has synchronized.
sections.eli5: Each message starts with a label: which version, what kind of message, did it work, and a ticket number so answers match questions.

sections.title: Connection Management
sections.content:
Connection messages are Add Branch (type 16), Delete Branch (17), Delete Tree (18), Verify Tree (19), Delete All (20) and Move Branch (22). They carry the port session number, input port with VPI/VCI, output port with VPI/VCI, a number of branches (used only by Verify Tree) and a priority.

GSMP makes no distinction between unicast and multicast. The first Add Branch for an input port, VPI and VCI makes a unicast connection. A second one with the same input turns it into a multicast connection with two branches, and so on. Deleting the last branch deletes the connection. All connections are unidirectional, from one input virtual channel to one or more output virtual channels.

A success response is a copy of the request with the Result set to Success. It must not be sent until the operation is done. A failure response is a copy with Result set to Failure and a failure code, and the switch state must not have changed. Repeating an Add Branch for an existing branch just reasserts the state or changes its priority.
sections.eli5: To connect a line, you say which incoming line goes to which outgoing line. Add another outgoing line and the same signal is copied to both, like a group call.

sections.title: Ports, Statistics, Configuration and Events
sections.content:
The Port Management message (type 32) has seven functions: Bring Up (1), Take Down (2), Internal Loopback (3), External Loopback (4), Bothway Loopback (5), Reset Input Port (6) and Reset Event Flags (7). Only Bring Up and Reset Input Port delete the connections on the input port, and only Bring Up changes the port session number.

Statistics messages (VC Activity 48, Port Statistics 49, VC Statistics 50) read hardware counters and tell whether a virtual channel has recently carried traffic. Configuration messages (Switch 64, Port 65, All Ports 66) let the controller discover what the switch can do, including how many priorities a port supports.

Event messages (types 80 to 84) are Port Up, Port Down, Invalid VPI/VCI, New Port and Dead Port. The switch sends them without waiting for an acknowledgement, and not during initialization.
sections.eli5: Besides connecting lines, the controller can switch a port on or off, test it by looping the signal back, ask for counts of what passed through, and ask what the switch can do.

sections.title: The Adjacency Protocol
sections.content:
Before anything else, the two ends run an adjacency protocol (message type 10) to synchronize state, learn the identity of the entity at the far end and detect when it changes. Its message carries a Code: SYN (1), SYNACK (2), ACK (3) or RSTACK (4), plus sender and receiver name (48 bits), port and instance number (32 bits).

An end starts in SYNSENT and reaches ESTAB when state synchronization is achieved. A timer drives periodic SYN, SYNACK or ACK messages depending on the state, and the RFC suggests one second. Instance numbers must change when a link or node comes back up, which is how a restart is detected. A mismatch is answered with RSTACK, which resets the link.
sections.eli5: It is a polite hello. Each side says who it is, the other repeats it back, and only then do they start giving real instructions. If one side forgets, they start the hello again.

sections.title: Failure Codes
sections.content:
A failure response returns the request with Result set to Failure (4) and a failure code in the Code field. The codes include 2 (invalid request message), 3 (not implemented on this switch), 4 (invalid port session number), 8 (connection does not exist), 9 (branch does not exist), 15 (out of resources) and 16 (failure specific to the particular message type).

Several codes cover limits of multicast support, for example when a switch can only support one branch of a multicast connection per output port. A switch must choose the most specific code. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: When the switch cannot do what it was asked, it sends the request back with a number saying why, such as no such line or out of room.

fields.name: Transaction Identifier
fields.desc: Matches a response to its request.

items.label: Add Branch
items.desc: Create a connection or add a branch.

items.label: Delete All
items.desc: Remove all connections on an input port.

items.label: Move Branch
items.desc: Replace one output branch with another.

items.label: Port Management
items.desc: Bring up, take down, loop back or reset a port.

items.label: VC Activity
items.desc: Report recent traffic on virtual channels.
